prompt: What does `go build -buildmode=plugin -o csv.so ./plugins/csv` produce, and how does a Go program use it?
hint: Two functions and one type make up the whole package.

choices.text: A Go source archive that the host compiles the first time it starts
choices.why: Nothing is compiled at run time. The file is already machine code; the host only maps it in.

choices.text: A shared object the host opens at run time and searches by name
choices.why: Right. The `.so` is loaded into the host's process, the `init` functions of its new packages run, and exported names are found by string.

choices.text: A separate executable that the host starts and feeds over a pipe
choices.why: That is the subprocess reporter of section 04. A plugin runs inside the host's own process.

choices.text: A static library linked into `hits-plugin` when it is built
choices.why: The host was built before the plugin and knows nothing about `csv.so` until it is named on the command line.

prompt: `plugins/csv/main.go` declares `var Reporter report.Reporter = csv.Reporter{}`. What is the dynamic type of the value `p.Lookup("Reporter")` returns?
hint: A variable and a function come back differently.

choices.text: `report.Reporter`
choices.why: That is the variable's type, but `Lookup` hands back the variable's address. Asserting `sym.(report.Reporter)` fails, because a pointer to an interface has no methods.

choices.text: `*report.Reporter`
choices.why: Right. A variable comes back as a pointer to the variable, so the host asserts `*report.Reporter` and dereferences it.

choices.text: `csv.Reporter`, the concrete type stored in the interface
choices.why: The host never sees the concrete type unless it digs into the interface; what `Lookup` returns is a pointer to the interface variable.

choices.text: `func() report.Reporter`
choices.why: That is what `plugins/mean` returns, because there `Reporter` is declared as a function.

prompt: `./hits-plugin access.log csv.so csv.so` printed 22 lines and `hits-plugin: registered [csv]`. `report.Register` panics on a duplicate name. Why did it not panic?
hint: Count how many times `init` ran, not how many times the reporter ran.

choices.text: `Register` silently ignores a second call that passes the very same reporter value
choices.why: `Register` panics on any name already in the map, whatever the value; section 02's file shows it.

choices.text: The second `.so` received a registry of its own
choices.why: There is one `report` package in the process, the host's. That is why the plugins' names appear in the host's registry at all.

choices.text: Opening a path again returns the plugin already loaded, without `init`
choices.why: Right. The reporter ran twice, so the CSV appears twice, but the plugin was initialised once.

choices.text: The host skips the second argument because it repeats the first
choices.why: The host loops over every argument and does run the reporter twice: 22 lines is the 11-line CSV twice.

prompt: Loading a shared object at run time is the C library's `dlopen`, so a host that imports `plugin` is dynamically linked: `readelf -d hits-plugin | grep NEEDED` prints `Shared library: [___]`.
hint: The one library every dynamically linked program on Linux asks for.

prompt: After `internal/tally/errors.go` added a method `Errors`, only the host was rebuilt, and the old `csv.so` failed with `plugin was built with a different version of package example.com/hits/internal/tally`. The CSV reporter never calls `Errors`. Why does it fail anyway?
hint: What does the runtime compare at `Open`, and for which packages?

choices.text: The runtime compares a hash of every package the two share, whether the plugin calls into it or not
choices.why: Right. The check is per shared package and runs before any `init`; one added method changes `tally`'s hash.

choices.text: `csv.so` calls `Errors` indirectly through `report`
choices.why: Neither `report` nor `reporters/csv` mentions `Errors`. The failure does not depend on any call.

choices.text: The host rebuilt `csv.so` automatically and the build failed
choices.why: The host never builds anything; it opened the file left from before, which is exactly the problem.

choices.text: A method on `Summary` changes the size of the struct
choices.why: A method adds no field, so the struct is the same size. The hash covers what the package exports, and that changed.

prompt: Which of these made `hits-plugin` refuse a plugin at `plugin.Open`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three refusals named a package deep in the runtime; two arrangements loaded fine.

choices.text: The host built with `-trimpath`, the plugin without
choices.why: Right: `different version of package internal/goarch`.

choices.text: The host built with `-race`, the plugin without
choices.why: Right: `different version of package internal/runtime/sys`.

choices.text: The plugin built with Go 1.27.2, the host with 1.27.1
choices.why: Right: one patch release apart, and the message names `internal/goarch`.

choices.text: Host and both plugins rebuilt after `errors.go` was added
choices.why: Built together from the same source, they loaded and printed `registered [csv mean]`.

choices.text: The same `csv.so` named twice on one command line
choices.why: The second open returned the plugin already in memory, and the CSV printed twice.

prompt: `go list -deps -buildmode=plugin ./plugins/csv` listed 69 packages and `go list -deps ./cmd/hits-plugin` listed 68. `comm -23` printed the three that only the plugin has. How many packages does `csv.so` share with the host?
hint: 69 minus the plugin's own.

prompt: A team builds its host with `CGO_ENABLED=0`, so that it fits a static image, and loads reporters from `.so` files that were built correctly on another machine. What happens?
hint: One of the four refusals in the section was not a build error.

choices.text: `go build` refuses: `-buildmode=plugin requires external (cgo) linking`
choices.why: That message is for building a plugin with cgo off. The host is an ordinary program and builds.

choices.text: It works, because each `.so` brings its own runtime
choices.why: A plugin's own copies of shared packages are never used, and here there is no loader to use them anyway: `Open` itself is a stub.

choices.text: It builds, and `plugin.Open` fails at run time with `plugin: not implemented`
choices.why: Right. Without cgo the `plugin` package compiles to stubs, so the mistake shows up only when the program runs.

choices.text: `plugin.Open` succeeds and `Lookup` fails for every symbol
choices.why: Both are stubs without cgo, and `Open` already returns the error.

prompt: A server has opened `reporter.so`. A bug is fixed, the same package is rebuilt to `reporter-v2.so`, and the server opens that file without restarting. What does it get?
hint: Think about how the runtime identifies a plugin.

choices.text: The new version, replacing the old one
choices.why: Nothing can be unloaded, and a second plugin with the same package path does not load beside the first.

choices.text: Both versions side by side, each with its own symbols
choices.why: That is what a new file name might suggest, but even a byte-identical copy was refused with `plugin already loaded`.

choices.text: An error, `plugin already loaded`
choices.why: Right. The plugin is identified by its package path, which is already in the process; only a new process can run the new version.

choices.text: The old version again, because `Open` caches by file contents
choices.why: The cache is by path; a new path is refused for another reason, its package path.

prompt: Given an empty log, `hits-plugin` died with exit status 2, while `hits-exec` reported `./mean-exec: exit status 2`, ran the Python reporter and exited with 1. What explains the difference?
hint: Both ran the same `mean` code with the same bug.

choices.text: `hits-exec` recovers panics and `hits-plugin` does not
choices.why: Neither host calls `recover`. The panic in `hits-exec`'s case happened in another process.

choices.text: The panic ran in the child, and the host only saw an exit status
choices.why: Right. In the plugin the same panic is the host's own; through `os/exec` it is one failed command.

choices.text: `GOTRACEBACK=none` turns the panic into an error in the subprocess
choices.why: It only shortens what the panic prints; the child still died with status 2.

choices.text: JSON cannot carry an empty summary, so `mean-exec` was never called
choices.why: It was called and it panicked: `panic: runtime error: integer divide by zero` is in the transcript.

prompt: `hits-exec` sends `{"protocol":1,"summary":…}` to each reporter. What is the number for?
hint: `echo '{"protocol":2}' | ./mean-exec` answered in a sentence.

choices.text: It tells the reporter which Go version built the host
choices.why: The reporter cannot and need not know that; no package is shared between the two processes.

choices.text: It numbers the reporters, so their output comes back in order
choices.why: Every reporter gets the same bytes, and the order comes from the loop over the arguments.

choices.text: The version of the message
choices.why: Right. `mean-exec` answered `protocol 2, and this reporter speaks 1` and exited with 1, instead of misreading the message.

choices.text: `encoding/json` requires a numeric first field
choices.why: JSON objects have no required fields at all; the field is the program's own decision.

prompt: `hits-static` never calls `report.Register`, yet `-r xml` answers `have [csv mean]`. How did the two reporters get into the registry?
hint: Look at the import block.

choices.text: `report` scans the module's `reporters` directory when the program starts
choices.why: A Go binary has no source tree to scan at run time; the registry only holds what code put there.

choices.text: The blank imports linked both packages in, and their `init` functions registered them at start-up
choices.why: Right. `import _` keeps a package for its side effect, and here the side effect is `Register`, as with `image/png`.

choices.text: `flag` loads the package named by `-r` when it parses the flag
choices.why: `flag` only stores a string. Nothing in Go loads a package by name at run time except `plugin`.

choices.text: `go generate` wrote the calls into `main.go`
choices.why: `go generate` could write the list of imports, but this file was written by hand and calls nothing.

prompt: Match each way of adding code from outside to the place the section names it.
hint: One description belongs to none of them.

pairs.left: a child process fed JSON on a pipe
one long-running plugin process called over RPC
a module run inside the host by a pure-Go runtime

prompt: In the benchmark, `BenchmarkProcess` took 1581082 ns/op and `BenchmarkCompiledIn` took 132.0 ns/op. Roughly how many times as expensive is a call through a new process? Give the nearest thousand.
hint: Divide the first by the second.

prompt: In `gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12`, `./hits-plugin` failed with `exec ./hits-plugin: no such file or directory`, though the file was mounted and `./hits-static` ran beside it. What was missing?
hint: `readelf -l hits-plugin | grep interpreter`.

choices.text: Execute permission on the mounted file
choices.why: A missing permission says `permission denied`, and `hits-static`, built the same way, ran.

choices.text: The dynamic loader `/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`, which the static image does not have
choices.why: Right. A dynamically linked program asks the kernel to run its interpreter first, and the error names the program because the interpreter is not there.

choices.text: The plugins, which were not copied into the image
choices.why: The whole directory was mounted, `csv.so` included; the program never started, so it never tried to open one.

choices.text: A network, because of `--network=none`
choices.why: None of these programs uses a network, and `hits-static` ran under the same flag.

prompt: A log shipper lets customers write filters in any language and replace them without restarting the shipper. A filter is called once per batch of about 5,000 events. Which design fits?
hint: Weigh each column of the table against the two requirements, then the call rate.

choices.text: Go plugins, because a call costs the same as a compiled-in one
choices.why: Customers would need the shipper's exact toolchain, flags and packages, filters would have to be in Go, and a new version is refused with `plugin already loaded`.

choices.text: Filters compiled into the shipper behind blank imports
choices.why: Fast and simple, but every new filter means rebuilding the shipper, which customers cannot do.

choices.text: Separate filter programs, each kept running and sent batches over a pipe or RPC
choices.why: Right. Any language, replaceable by starting the new program, and a long-lived process pays its start once rather than per batch.

choices.text: A new process for every event, as `hits-exec` does
choices.why: The shape is right but the rate is not: about 1.6 ms per process start, 5,000 times per batch, is about eight seconds per batch.

prompt: `BenchmarkPlugin` measured 136.1 ns/op and `BenchmarkCompiledIn` 132.0 ns/op. What is the right reading?
hint: What is a plugin's `Report` once `Lookup` has returned?

choices.text: Every plugin call goes through `dlsym`, which costs about four nanoseconds
choices.why: The symbol is resolved once, in `Lookup`; the loop afterwards never touches the loader.

choices.text: The plugin is 3 per cent slower and should be avoided in a hot loop
choices.why: Three per cent between two benchmark runs is noise that another run can close or reverse.

choices.text: The same cost: after `Lookup`, both are an interface call
choices.why: Right. Speed is the plugin's real advantage, and the compiled-in reporter has it too.

choices.text: The plugin's copy of `fmt` is slower than the host's
choices.why: The plugin's own copies of shared packages are not used; its calls go to the host's `fmt`.

prompt: Put in order what happens when `hits-plugin` loads `csv.so` and uses it.
hint: The hash check comes before any code from the plugin runs.
items: the runtime compares the hash of every shared package with the host's
the `init` functions of the new packages run, and `csv` registers itself
the host dereferences it and calls `Report`

prompt: CI builds the host with `go build -trimpath` from tag v2.3.0. A plugin author checks out the same tag, runs plain `go build -buildmode=plugin` with the same Go 1.27.1, and `plugin.Open` fails naming `internal/goarch`. What fixes it?
hint: Same source and same toolchain were not enough in section 03.

choices.text: Upgrade both the host and the plugin to the next Go release
choices.why: A new release changes nothing about the mismatch; the flags would still differ.

choices.text: Build the plugin with the host's exact flags
choices.why: Right. `-trimpath` changes how every package is compiled, so the plugin needs it too; building both in one job keeps every flag equal.

choices.text: Delete `internal/goarch` from the plugin package's import list
choices.why: Nobody imports it directly; it is part of the runtime every Go program carries.

choices.text: Set `GOTOOLCHAIN=local` on the machine where the plugin author builds
choices.why: Both already used 1.27.1; the toolchain is not what differs.

prompt: `import _ "image/png"` keeps the package only for its side effect: its ___ function calls `image.RegisterFormat("png", …)`, the same way `reporters/csv` registers itself in `report`.
hint: The function that runs before `main` and that `plugin.Open` also runs.
